checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-008: Is RANDOM_CHALLENGE_KZG_CELL_BATCH_DOMAIN globally unique and collision-free across all protocol contexts?

audit_items.state_context: Domain separator RANDOM_CHALLENGE_KZG_CELL_BATCH_DOMAIN = b'RCKZGCBATCH__V1_' (fulu fork). Related: RANDOM_CHALLENGE_KZG_BATCH_DOMAIN = b'RCKZGBATCH___V1_' (deneb), FIAT_SHAMIR_PROTOCOL_DOMAIN = b'FSBLOBVERIFY_V1_' (deneb). All distinct at byte level.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The domain separator RCKZGCBATCH__V1_ is a 16-byte static constant compiled into c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1. It differs from the Deneb blob-batch domain RCKZGBATCH___V1_ by the inclusion of a C character and different underscore count. The constant is not configurable at runtime. Prysm uses the c-kzg-4844 library without any Go-layer domain validation or override.
state_anomalies_found: No runtime modification path for domain constant
Visual similarity to Deneb blob-batch domain may cause developer confusion but does not create a collision
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No domain-related state or caching. Domain is a compile-time constant with no mutable state.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Domain constant is read-only; no race conditions possible.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No exploit path exists to confuse domain separators via P2P inputs. The domain is hardcoded in the C library binary and cannot be overridden by any attacker-controlled input. SHA-256 collision resistance prevents any cross-domain forgery.
attack_scenarios: Cross-domain replay from Deneb blob-batch (rejected: different Go API functions)
Future version confusion _V2_ vs _V1_ (rejected: same library version pinned per node)
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None. Domain is stateless and constant.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The domain is not reachable from any P2P or RPC path as an input parameter. It is embedded in the C binary. Attacker controls commitments, cells, proofs, and indices but not the domain.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No attack surface for domain confusion. Attacker cannot modify domain separator through network inputs.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant that RCKZGCBATCH__V1_ is globally unique among deployed Ethereum KZG protocols is proven. All three KZG domain strings (FSBLOBVERIFY_V1_, RCKZGBATCH___V1_, RCKZGCBATCH__V1_) differ in bytes at positions 4-11. SHA-256 preimage resistance ensures domain isolation. The assert in C code provides a runtime check on domain string length.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Static C constant RANDOM_CHALLENGE_DOMAIN_VERIFY_CELL_KZG_PROOF_BATCH plus runtime assert on length
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient. The domain is not attacker-controlled and differs from all other deployed domains at the byte level.
edge_cases: Future fork adds a new domain identical to this one (version governance issue, not a current vulnerability)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The domain separator is correctly implemented, unique, and not attacker-controllable. No exploitable vulnerability exists.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Consider adding a test that asserts the byte-by-byte distinctness of all KZG domain separators as a regression guard.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Does P2P gossip validation reject proofs generated with foreign domain separators?

audit_items.state_context: P2P path: validateDataColumn -> validateWithKzgBatchVerifier -> verifyKzgBatch -> VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs -> kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch -> C library. Zero-cell batch edge case: C function returns ok=true without crypto check. Mitigated by upstream ValidFields -> VerifyDataColumnSidecar check.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Foreign-domain proofs are 48-byte G1 curve points that pass syntactic validation but fail the pairing equation when verified under RCKZGCBATCH__V1_. The domain enforcement is cryptographic, embedded in the Fiat-Shamir challenge derivation in the C library. Zero-cell batch edge: C function returns ok=true without any pairing check; mitigated by ValidFields upstream.
state_anomalies_found: Zero-cell batch returns ok=true without cryptographic verification (mitigated by upstream ValidFields check)
No explicit foreign-domain detection at the Go layer — relies entirely on cryptographic pairing failure
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of domain-related state. Each verification is fresh.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Domain rejection occurs in the C library which uses per-invocation state only. No concurrency issues.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Submitting a proof computed under any domain other than RCKZGCBATCH__V1_ results in a different Fiat-Shamir challenge r, causing the linear combination pairing equation to fail. The probability of accidental acceptance is approximately 1/BLS_field_order < 2^-255.
attack_scenarios: Submit Deneb blob-batch proof as cell proof: rejected by pairing check
Submit arbitrary G1 point as proof: rejected by pairing check
Submit zero-length batch to bypass crypto check: blocked by ValidFields upstream check

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Attacker can reach the KZG verifier through P2P gossip on data_column_sidecar subnets. All bytes of the cells, commitments, and proofs are attacker-controlled. Domain rejection is cryptographically enforced.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can send arbitrary 48-byte proofs and 4096-byte cells. Will always be rejected by pairing check unless attacker breaks BLS discrete log.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant holds cryptographically. The only concern is the zero-cell bypass, but it is mitigated by the upstream ValidFields check. The pairing equation provides the foreign-domain rejection guarantee.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Fiat-Shamir challenge r computed under RCKZGCBATCH__V1_ domain; pairings_verify check
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for cryptographic rejection. The zero-cell edge case is mitigated upstream.
edge_cases: Zero-cell batch: C function returns ok=true without crypto check. Mitigated by upstream ValidFields. Direct call to VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs with empty sidecars produces count=0 which passes vacuously.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Foreign-domain rejection is cryptographically sound. The zero-cell edge case is mitigated by the existing validation chain.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Consider adding an explicit check in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs to reject empty batches rather than relying on upstream validators.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Do validators correctly apply domain separator before attesting to blocks with data columns?

audit_items.state_context: Both P2P gossip and sync/RPC paths converge on peerdas.VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs. The domain separator is a compile-time constant in c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1 with no runtime override.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: All verification paths (P2P gossip, sync, RPC) in Prysm converge on the same peerdas.VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs function and the same C library call. The domain separator is a compile-time constant with no configurable override. No divergence in domain usage was found.
state_anomalies_found: None. All paths use identical domain.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No domain-related caching. No state divergence possible.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Domain is a read-only constant. No concurrency concerns.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No counterexample found. Domain consistency is guaranteed by all verification paths calling the same underlying C function. Version mismatch between nodes is the only theoretical scenario, not a code defect.
attack_scenarios: Version mismatch between nodes running different c-kzg-4844 versions (operational, not code defect)
Malicious fork of c-kzg-4844 with changed domain (supply chain attack, out of scope)

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The domain is not externally reachable or modifiable. All verification paths use the same function.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Invariant proven by code inspection. All three verification entry points call peerdas.VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs which delegates to the same C function with the same hardcoded domain. No configuration or runtime override exists.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Single implementation path: all calls route through peerdas.VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs
edge_cases: Dependency version upgrade could silently change domain; no cross-check in Go layer

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Validators use identical domain separators. No vulnerability.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Add integration test asserting domain separator value across all verification code paths as regression guard.

checklist_item.title: Verify Domain Separator Construction: Is RANDOM_CHALLENGE_KZG_CELL_BATCH_DOMAIN derived using a collision-resistant method?

audit_items.state_context: hash_to_bls_field uses modular reduction (not rejection sampling). Creates ~9% bias from 2^256 mod BLS_field_order mapping. This is ~28% probability difference for the overrepresented range. Intentional design per EIP-7594 spec.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The domain separator is not derived but is a static constant used as a prefix input to SHA-256. The resulting 256-bit hash is reduced modulo the BLS12-381 field order via blst_fr_from_scalar. This creates a ~9% modular bias in the output field element. The derivation method uses SHA-256 which provides 128-bit collision resistance.
state_anomalies_found: hash_to_bls_field uses modular reduction (not rejection sampling), creating ~9% distributional bias. Cryptographically negligible for security proofs but technically not uniform.
No Go-layer validation that SHA-256 output is in BLS field before reduction.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of derived values across calls. Each verification recomputes r from scratch.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No shared mutable state in the derivation. Thread-safe.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: The modular reduction bias in hash_to_bls_field is approximately 9% and is not exploitable in practice. SHA-256 collision resistance prevents finding two distinct inputs that produce the same r value. No practical attack path exists.
attack_scenarios: Exploit hash_to_bls_field bias to predict r: requires SHA-256 preimage computation (2^128 work)
SHA-256 collision to create two inputs with same r: requires 2^128 work, infeasible

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The derivation function is called internally by verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch. Attacker can influence the hash input but cannot exploit the negligible bias.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can influence hash inputs but cannot exploit the negligible bias or break SHA-256.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The derivation is collision-resistant by SHA-256 properties. The modular bias is acceptable per EIP-7594 specification, consistent with standard hash-to-field practices. No gap in the guard exists.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: SHA-256 as hash function with 128-bit collision resistance; BLS field reduction mod field_order
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient. The bias is within the security margin.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The derivation method is collision-resistant. The modular reduction bias is negligible and consistent with specification requirements.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. Note: hash_to_bls_field intentionally differs from bytes_to_bls_field by omitting the range check; this is correct behavior for hash-to-field.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-008: Is hash input order in compute_verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_challenge deterministic and canonical?

audit_items.state_context: Hash input order (fixed in C): domain(16) || FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL(8) || num_commitments(8) || num_cells(8) || unique_commitments || commitment_indices || cell_indices || cells || proofs. Ordering of batched items in verifyKzgBatch depends on goroutine scheduling order, but this is benign since verifier re-derives r from received data.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The hash input ordering in compute_r_powers_for_verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch is deterministic for any fixed input array ordering. The ordering of batched items in verifyKzgBatch depends on goroutine scheduling order, but this does not create a vulnerability because the verifier always re-derives r from the cells it holds. Different orderings produce different r values but consistently verify the same cell set.
state_anomalies_found: Ordering of cells in combined batch (verifyKzgBatch) depends on goroutine scheduling non-determinism
Different ordering produces different r, but verification remains consistent per-batch
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No ordering-related caching. Each batch re-derives r.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Goroutine scheduling causes non-deterministic batch composition ordering. This is benign because r is derived from received data, not from a pre-agreed ordering.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No exploit path found. Ordering non-determinism in batch composition does not allow forged proof acceptance because the verifier always re-derives r from the exact ordered inputs it processes. A prover cannot predict r to craft a forgery since r depends on the received cells.
attack_scenarios: Submit cells in different ordering than expected: verifier re-derives r from received ordering, still verifies correctly
Race condition in batch composition to influence r: even if r is influenced, valid proofs remain valid and invalid proofs remain invalid
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: Batch composition ordering depends on goroutine scheduling, but this is benign.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: P2P attacker sends single sidecars; ordering within a sidecar is deterministic (sequential range loop). Batch ordering across goroutines is determined by channel receive order. Attacker cannot exploit this ordering variation.
entry_points: P2P gossip: validateDataColumn sends single-item batches
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Ordering is influenced by goroutine scheduling, not by attacker inputs.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant holds. The hash input ordering is deterministic for a fixed input array. The Fiat-Shamir transform is correct: r is derived from the verifier's received data, not pre-agreed, so ordering variation does not compromise soundness.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Sequential memcpy/bytes_from_uint64 with fixed buffer layout in compute_r_powers_for_verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch
edge_cases: Combining cells from multiple sidecars: ordering depends on channel drain order; benign

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Hash input ordering is deterministic per invocation. Batch composition ordering variation is benign because r is verifier-derived. No exploit path.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Do validators compute identical Fiat-Shamir challenges when verifying the same data column proofs?

audit_items.code_snippet:
// SSZ deserialization is canonical. Sequential iteration over sidecar.Column produces deterministic input arrays.
// All validators processing same sidecar produce same commitments/indices/cells/proofs arrays.
audit_items.state_context: SSZ deserialization is canonical in Prysm. The inner loop for i := range sidecar.Column iterates in 0,1,2... order deterministically. FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL is a fixed constant. Domain is a fixed constant.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Validators receiving identical sidecar bytes compute identical Fiat-Shamir challenges because: (1) the domain is a fixed constant, (2) FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL is a fixed constant, (3) all other inputs are deterministically derived from the SSZ-deserialized sidecar, and (4) the iteration order over sidecar.Column is deterministic (sequential index).
state_anomalies_found: None found. Challenge derivation is deterministic given identical inputs.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of challenges. Each call is fresh.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Each validation goroutine operates on its own copy of the sidecar data. No shared mutable state.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No divergence scenario found. SSZ deserialization is canonical; sidecar field ordering is fixed by the protobuf/SSZ schema. All validators processing the same sidecar produce the same input arrays.
attack_scenarios: Non-canonical SSZ encoding: rejected by SSZ decoder before reaching KZG
Sidecar with duplicate commitment bytes: deduplicate_commitments handles this deterministically

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Challenge computation is internal to verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch. No external influence on ordering possible for P2P single-sidecar path.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No attack surface for challenge divergence.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Invariant proven. Identical sidecar inputs produce identical challenges. No divergence path found.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Deterministic SSZ deserialization + sequential iteration + fixed constants
edge_cases: Batch verification combining sidecars from different sources could produce different orderings, but this is benign per CHK-0085 analysis

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Validators compute identical challenges for identical sidecars. No vulnerability.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Are hash inputs canonicalized before feeding to compute_verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_challenge?

audit_items.state_context: BLS12-381 G1 compressed points have unique canonical encoding. uint64 values use big-endian 8-byte encoding. Cell bytes are raw arrays. Non-G1 commitment bytes cause error returns (C_KZG_BADARGS propagated as Go error), not false-positive verifications.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Hash inputs use deterministic encodings: uint64 values use big-endian 8-byte format, commitments and proofs use BLS12-381 compressed G1 point format (unique representation), cells are raw byte arrays. Commitments are validated as valid G1 points after hashing (not before), meaning non-G1 commitment bytes would be hashed but then cause an error in later processing. This does not create a canonicalization vulnerability.
state_anomalies_found: Commitments are hashed before G1 point validation; non-G1 byte strings would be hashed but cause error returns later
Cell bytes are not individually validated as BLS field elements before hashing; non-field-order values are hashed as-is but cause arithmetic errors in interpolation poly computation
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of hash inputs or derived challenges.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No shared state in hash input construction.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No canonicalization exploit found. BLS12-381 compressed G1 points have unique encodings. SHA-256 collision resistance prevents two different byte strings from producing the same challenge. Non-canonical bytes cause error returns, not false positive verifications.
attack_scenarios: Submit non-G1 bytes as commitment: hashed into challenge, then causes C_KZG_BADARGS error return (not false-positive accept)
Submit cell bytes with values >= BLS field order: hashed as-is, causes arithmetic errors in interpolation poly, propagated as error

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Attacker can submit arbitrary 48-byte commitment values and 4096-byte cell values. Non-G1 commitment bytes cause error returns propagating through the stack. Non-field-order cell bytes cause arithmetic errors in the interpolation polynomial computation.
entry_points: P2P gossip with attacker-controlled commitment/cell bytes
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can submit any bytes for commitments, cells, and proofs. All invalid combinations cause error returns, not false accepts.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant holds. Canonical encodings are enforced: G1 points have unique compressed form, integers use fixed-width big-endian encoding. Non-canonical cell bytes produce different hash outputs and cause arithmetic errors in later processing (causing error returns, not bypasses).
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Unique BLS12-381 G1 compressed point encoding; fixed-width big-endian integer encoding; SHA-256 preimage resistance
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for the protocol's security requirements.
edge_cases: Future ECC library allowing alternative G1 point encodings could break uniqueness guarantee (library-level concern)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Hash inputs are sufficiently canonicalized. Non-canonical inputs cause error returns, not false-positive verifications.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Consider adding explicit pre-validation of commitment bytes before hashing as a defense-in-depth measure.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-002: Is the universal verification equation e(LL, LR) == e(RL, [1]) correctly implemented in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl?

audit_items.state_context: G1_INFINITY commitments accepted by validate_kzg_g1 (blst_p1_is_inf returns true). All-infinity inputs produce e(0,[1])==e(0,[s^n]) = 1_GT == 1_GT = true. Mitigated by block-level commitment validation and Merkle inclusion proof requiring non-trivial commitments.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The pairing equation e(final_g1_sum, [1]) == e(proof_lincomb, [s^n]) is correctly implemented. final_g1_sum aggregates commitment_sum - interpolation_polynomial_commit + weighted_proof_sum. The negation of interpolation_poly_commit is explicit via blst_p1_cneg. power_of_s is correctly read from trusted setup at index FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL.
state_anomalies_found: G1_INFINITY inputs accepted by validate_kzg_g1; if all pairing arguments are infinity, pairing equals GT identity (1_GT == 1_GT = true). Requires crafting commitment/proof sums to zero which needs breaking KZG binding.
Trusted setup integrity: if g2_values_monomial[FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL] is incorrect, all cell verifications fail silently.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: pairings_verify operates on local variables only. Thread-safe.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No exploit path found to satisfy the pairing equation with invalid proofs. The infinity-point false-positive scenario requires a block with all-infinity KZG commitments (a consistently zeroed block) which would be rejected at block validation level before generating valid sidecars.
attack_scenarios: All-infinity commitments/proofs: passes pairing check vacuously. Requires block with all-infinity KZG commitments + valid proposer signature + valid Merkle proof. Blocked by transaction-level blob validation requiring non-trivial commitments.
Incorrect power_of_s index: only possible if FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL > trusted setup length (impossible for valid Ethereum trusted setup)

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The infinity-point scenario requires: (1) all commitments G1_INFINITY, (2) all proofs G1_INFINITY, (3) zero interpolation polynomial, (4) valid Merkle inclusion proof for all-infinity block commitments. Conditions (1-4) would form a consistent but trivially invalid block rejected at block validation.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Infinity-point scenario is reachable from P2P but blocked by block-level commitment validation.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The pairing equation is correctly implemented and matches the EIP-7594 specification. The infinity-point concern requires a consistently zeroed block rejected at block validation level. The blst library's pairings_verify correctly implements the Miller loop and final exponentiation.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: pairings_verify using blst_miller_loop_n and blst_fp12_finalverify; negation via blst_p1_cneg
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient. Minor defense-in-depth concern around infinity points.
edge_cases: All-infinity commitments: pass G1 validation but create trivially invalid blocks

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Pairing equation is correctly implemented. The infinity-point defense-in-depth concern requires a coordinated attack at multiple validation layers which is prevented by upstream checks.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. The infinity-point scenario is mitigated by upstream block validation.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Does the random challenge r in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl have sufficient entropy to prevent proof forgery?

audit_items.state_context: r is Fiat-Shamir derived, not random. hash_to_bls_field uses modular reduction (not rejection sampling). Values in [0, 2^256 mod p - 1] are ~2x more likely. This creates ~9% bias. 128-bit security maintained.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The random challenge r is derived via SHA-256 (256-bit output) reduced modulo the BLS12-381 field order p (~2^254.86). Since 2^256/p ~2.2, the modular reduction creates approximately 9% non-uniformity bias. Effective entropy is approximately 253 bits. This is sufficient for the protocol's 128-bit security target but is not perfectly uniform.
state_anomalies_found: ~9% distributional bias in r from modular reduction (not rejection sampling)
Effective entropy of r is ~253 bits, not the full BLS field size
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: r is recomputed fresh each invocation. No caching.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: SHA-256 computation is deterministic and stateless. No concurrency issues.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: The ~9% bias in r is not exploitable in practice. Exploiting it would require an attacker to predict the range of r before committing to their cells and proofs, which is impossible since r depends on the attacker's inputs. The protocol security holds at 128-bit level despite the bias.
attack_scenarios: Exploit bias to increase collision probability: requires 2^128 / 1.09 ~2^127.5 work — negligible improvement
Attacker crafts cells/proofs to land in biased r range: circular dependency since r depends on submitted cells/proofs

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The bias in r is not exploitable from any attack surface. The attacker controls the hash inputs but cannot predict r without computing SHA-256.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No exploitable attack surface for bias exploitation.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: r has sufficient entropy (~253 effective bits) for the 128-bit security requirement. The modular bias is a known property of hash-to-field without rejection sampling and is accepted by the EIP-7594 specification. The Schwartz-Zippel lemma provides security for the RLC with high probability even with this bias.
edge_cases: Future theoretical attack exploiting SHA-256 non-randomness or BLS field structure to leverage the bias (theoretical, not practical)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: r has sufficient entropy. The modular reduction bias is a known, accepted tradeoff in hash-to-field constructions. 128-bit security level is maintained.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. For future hardening, consider using hash_to_field with rejection sampling per RFC 9380.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Are RLC, RLI, and RLP components in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl computed correctly from cells and commitments?

audit_items.state_context: sidecar.Index = column index (uint64). All cells in a DataColumnSidecar share the same column index but have different commitments (one per blob). Commitment deduplication: when same commitment appears for multiple cells, weights are accumulated. reverse-bit-limited cell indices used for coset factor computation.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: RLC, RLI, and RLP are computed correctly. Commitment deduplication correctly accumulates r-power weights. The column index (sidecar.Index) is correctly used as the cell_index for all cells in a sidecar (all cells of a column share the same column index). The coset shift powers h_k^n are correctly derived via get_coset_shift_pow_for_cell using reverse-bit-limited cell indices. No arithmetic bugs found in the three components.
state_anomalies_found: Commitment deduplication order: commitments are deduplicated by byte comparison in order of appearance; the resulting commitment_indices correctly map each cell to its unique commitment.
N cells from same column (same sidecar.Index) are correctly handled: same column_index in cell_indices, different commitments, correct coset factor applied to all.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of RLC components between calls.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: All computations are per-invocation. No shared mutable state.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No arithmetic exploit found. Forging an RLC-consistent proof for invalid cells requires breaking KZG binding. The column index correctly constrains the coset used for evaluation, preventing cross-column attacks.
attack_scenarios: Submit cells from column 3 with column 5 index: coset factor mismatch causes pairing check failure
Submit cells with wrong commitment mapping: commitment_indices deduplication is deterministic and correct

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Attacker controls all input values (column index, cells, commitments, proofs). All invalid combinations cause pairing check failure with high probability.
entry_points: P2P: VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs with sidecar.Index as cell_index
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can submit any column index, but incorrect column index causes pairing failure.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: RLC components are correctly computed per EIP-7594. Commitment deduplication is correct. Column index usage is correct. Coset factor derivation matches the EIP specification.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: compute_weighted_sum_of_commitments, compute_commitment_to_aggregated_interpolation_poly, computed_weighted_sum_of_proofs — all matching EIP-7594 spec
edge_cases: Single-cell batch: r^0 = 1, pairing check is equivalent to single-cell KZG verification. Correct.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: RLC components are correctly implemented. No vulnerability.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Do actor-p2p-peer and actor-validator-node correctly invoke verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl before accepting data column sidecars?

audit_items.state_context: Batch verifier sends SAME error to ALL co-batched goroutines when ANY sidecar fails. Each goroutine falls back to individual validation. Timeout=SecondsPerSlot. On timeout, returns ValidationIgnore WITHOUT recording in seenDataColumnCache. Invalid sidecar from malicious validator causes O(batch_size) individual re-verifications. seenDataColumnCache is populated at step 13 (AFTER KZG at step 12), meaning timeout during fallback prevents cache entry creation.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Both P2P gossip (validateWithKzgBatchVerifier) and sync (SidecarKzgProofVerified) paths correctly invoke KZG verification before accepting sidecars. The batch verifier sends the same error to all co-batched goroutines when any sidecar fails, triggering individual fallback verification for all of them. This creates a DoS amplification scenario where one invalid sidecar causes O(batch_size) individual re-verifications, potentially causing timeout-based ValidationIgnore for honest sidecars.
state_anomalies_found: verifyKzgBatch sends SAME error to ALL co-batched goroutines regardless of which sidecar caused the batch failure
Timeout-based ValidationIgnore: if fallback verification exceeds SecondsPerSlot, honest sidecars are silently dropped without being recorded in seenDataColumnCache
seenDataColumnCache populated at step 13 (after KZG step 12) — timeout during fallback prevents cache entry, allowing replay in same slot
kzgVerifierRoutine drains kzgChan non-deterministically, combining items from different goroutines without attribution
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: seenDataColumnCache is checked AFTER KZG verification (step 13). A sidecar that passes batch KZG but then times out during fallback re-verification would not be cached, allowing replay. The cache key is (slot, proposerIndex, columnIndex) — no KZG proof hash, so a different invalid sidecar with same slot/proposer/column could repeatedly poison the batch.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: kzgVerifierRoutine drains kzgChan non-deterministically. Multiple goroutines from different P2P messages can be combined in the same batch. One failing sidecar affects all co-batched goroutines. This is a concurrency design flaw in the batch error attribution.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: A malicious validator with a valid key can submit a DataColumnSidecar with valid BLS signature and valid Merkle inclusion proof but invalid KZG cells/proofs. This sidecar passes all pre-KZG checks (steps 1-11) but fails at step 12. When batched with honest sidecars, ALL co-batched goroutines receive the failure and fall back to individual re-verification. Under sustained attack (each slot), this creates persistent availability degradation for PeerDAS data columns.
phase2_symbolic_execution.counterexample: Attack: Malicious proposer at slot N creates a DataColumnSidecar with valid BLS proposer signature, valid KZG commitment Merkle inclusion proof (commitments match block body), but invalid KZG cells (cells do not correspond to the committed polynomial). Sidecar passes steps 1-11. At step 12 (validateWithKzgBatchVerifier), the sidecar is combined in a batch with K honest sidecars. The combined batch fails. ALL K+1 goroutines receive ValidationError and fall back to validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg. If K is large (busy slot), individual fallback verifications collectively take > SecondsPerSlot. Honest sidecars receive ValidationIgnore. seenDataColumnCache is not populated for ignored sidecars. Attack repeats each slot with minimal cost (one sidecar per slot per column). Impact: nodes miss PeerDAS data columns, degrading data availability sampling.
attack_scenarios: Malicious proposer submits column sidecar with valid proposer signature + valid Merkle proof + invalid KZG cells: causes batch failure affecting all co-batched honest sidecars
Attacker floods each subnet with invalid-KZG sidecars from different compromised validator keys to saturate kzgChan and cause systematic timeout-based ignores
Context timeout path: if parent context canceled (node under load), ValidationIgnore returned without KZG result, potentially allowing replay of the honest sidecar
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: Attack requires the invalid sidecar to be batched with honest sidecars within the kzgVerifierRoutine's drain window (determined by goroutine scheduling). The timeout threshold (SecondsPerSlot) is the key parameter.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The fallback path is fully reachable from P2P gossip. The attacker needs a valid validator key to produce sidecars that pass BLS signature (step 8) and Merkle proof (step 11) checks before reaching KZG. Without a valid key, sidecars are rejected before the batch verifier.
entry_points: P2P gossip: validateDataColumn -> validateWithKzgBatchVerifier -> fallback validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Requires valid validator key. Attacker is a malicious/compromised proposer or validator who can produce valid-seeming but KZG-invalid sidecars. Cost: one validator key, one sidecar per column per slot.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The security invariant 'no false-positive KZG acceptance' holds — no sidecar bypasses KZG verification. However, the liveness invariant 'no false-negative rejection of valid sidecars' can be violated under adversarial timing. The batch-to-individual fallback design has a fundamental attribution problem: one invalid sidecar penalizes all co-batched goroutines. The timeout path creates a window where honest sidecars are dropped/ignored rather than accepted.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: validateWithKzgBatchVerifier with fallback to validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg; SidecarKzgProofVerified in beacon-chain/verification
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Security guard (no false accepts) is SUFFICIENT. Liveness guard (no false ignores under adversarial conditions) has a WEAKNESS: timeout causes ValidationIgnore for honest sidecars co-batched with an attacker's invalid sidecar.
edge_cases: Context timeout during fallback: honest sidecar gets ValidationIgnore, no re-processing guarantee, no cache entry
Batch composed entirely of invalid sidecars: all get error, all fall back individually, all correctly rejected
Single-item batch with invalid sidecar: only that sidecar falls back, no collateral damage (the vulnerability only manifests in multi-item batches)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: A malicious validator can exploit the batch fallback mechanism to cause liveness disruption: honest sidecars co-batched with an attacker's invalid sidecar may receive ValidationIgnore under load, degrading PeerDAS data availability sampling. The attack requires a valid validator key but has persistent per-slot impact at minimal cost. The seenDataColumnCache non-population for ignored sidecars allows per-slot replay amplification.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Fix: In verifyKzgBatch, identify which sidecar(s) caused the batch failure using binary search or per-sidecar retry, and only trigger the fallback for the failing sidecar(s). Alternatively, use per-item error channels rather than broadcasting the same error to all goroutines. Also: populate seenDataColumnCache immediately on valid BLS signature + Merkle proof pass (steps 7-11) to prevent replay amplification.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.severity_estimate: Medium — liveness/availability attack on PeerDAS data column propagation, requires valid validator key, persistent per-slot impact

vulnerability_details.title: Batch KZG Verifier Error Attribution: One Invalid Sidecar Causes O(n) Collateral Fallback, Enabling PeerDAS Liveness Attack
vulnerability_details.root_cause: verifyKzgBatch sends the same combined error to all co-batched goroutines regardless of which specific sidecar caused the batch failure. This creates O(n) fallback overhead from a single invalid sidecar. Under load, individual fallback verifications can exceed the SecondsPerSlot timeout, causing honest sidecars to receive ValidationIgnore without cache entry creation.
exploit_preconditions: Valid validator key or compromised proposer
Ability to publish DataColumnSidecar with valid BLS signature + Merkle proof but invalid KZG cells
vulnerability_details.impact: PeerDAS data availability degradation: nodes systematically miss data column sidecars during adversarial slots, reducing the effectiveness of data availability sampling

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-002/tb-008: Does hash_to_bls_field produce uniformly random BLS field elements with full ~2^255 bit entropy?

audit_items.state_context: hash_to_bls_field uses modular reduction (blst_fr_from_scalar) without rejection sampling. bytes_to_bls_field uses blst_scalar_fr_check which validates scalar is in [0, p-1]. ~9% bias from 2^256 mod p ≈ 2^1.14 * p. Computationally indistinguishable from uniform under SHA-256 pseudorandomness.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: hash_to_bls_field interprets a 32-byte big-endian value as a 256-bit integer and reduces it mod p via blst_fr_from_scalar. Since SHA-256 output is 256 bits and p ~2^254.86, the reduction creates approximately 9% statistical non-uniformity. The output is NOT perfectly uniform but is computationally indistinguishable from uniform. This intentionally differs from bytes_to_bls_field which enforces range checking but can fail.
state_anomalies_found: ~9% statistical bias in output distribution (values in [0, 2^256 mod p - 1] are ~2x more likely)
No range check or rejection sampling — intentional design choice for hash-to-field contexts
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching. Each call produces an independent (biased) field element.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: The bias is not exploitable without SHA-256 preimage computation. An attacker cannot craft inputs to select specific biased values. The computational indistinguishability from uniform is sufficient for the security proof.
attack_scenarios: Distinguish biased from uniform outputs: requires exponential samples, infeasible
Craft SHA-256 preimage to force specific r: requires 2^128 work, infeasible

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: hash_to_bls_field is called internally with the SHA-256 hash of attacker-influenced data. The attacker cannot select which biased values are output.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No exploitable attack surface for bias exploitation.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The function produces computationally indistinguishable-from-uniform outputs under SHA-256 pseudorandomness. The ~9% statistical bias is not exploitable by computationally bounded adversaries. The invariant holds in the standard computational security model.
edge_cases: Statistical bias becomes exploitable if SHA-256 is significantly weakened in future (theoretical)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The non-uniformity is a known, accepted property of hash-to-field without rejection sampling. Computationally indistinguishable from uniform. No exploitable vulnerability.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. For information: rejection-sampling-based hash_to_field per RFC 9380 section 5 would provide true uniformity but requires protocol specification change.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Does the Fiat-Shamir challenge r correctly bind ALL inputs in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl?

audit_items.state_context: num_commitments is post-deduplication count. Length fields (num_commitments, num_cells) prevent extension/truncation attacks. Block-level context (block root, slot, proposer) validated by ValidProposerSignature (step 8) and SidecarInclusionProven (step 11) upstream.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: r correctly binds all cryptographically relevant inputs: domain, FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_CELL, num_commitments (post-deduplication), num_cells, all unique commitments, all commitment_indices, all cell_indices, all cells, and all proofs. Block-level context is NOT bound in r, but this is correct: block context is validated separately by BLS signature and Merkle inclusion proof.
state_anomalies_found: num_commitments in hash is post-deduplication, not original input length; deterministic and correct
Block root/slot/proposer not bound in r; correct since these are validated by separate checks upstream
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching. r binds to specific cell set each invocation.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: All prover-controlled inputs are bound. No missing binding found. Cross-block replay of KZG proofs is theoretically possible but prevented by the BLS signature and Merkle inclusion checks at higher layers.
attack_scenarios: Cross-block replay of valid KZG proof: prevented by BLS signature validation requiring correct proposer key for the specific block
Submit duplicate commitments to reduce num_commitments: deterministic deduplication, no exploitable ambiguity

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: All relevant inputs are bound in r. No missing binding exploitable from P2P interface.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker controls committed inputs but cannot exploit any missing binding.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The binding is complete for the algebraic KZG check. Length prefixes prevent extension attacks. The deduplication-based num_commitments is deterministic and correct. Block-level context binding is correctly delegated to BLS signature and Merkle proof checks.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: SHA-256 over domain || constants || length-prefixed inputs || all content
edge_cases: If deduplication logic has a bug, wrong num_commitments could be hashed; code inspection shows no bug

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: r correctly binds all prover-controlled inputs. The complete binding is achieved by the combination of KZG Fiat-Shamir + BLS signature + Merkle proof.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Is the random challenge r resistant to attacker influence through crafted P2P inputs?

audit_items.state_context: Attacker has full control over hash inputs but cannot exploit this to bypass the pairing check without breaking SHA-256 preimage resistance (128-bit security). G1_INFINITY all-zero commitments/proofs: pairing check vacuously true but blocked by SidecarInclusionProven requiring commitments to match block body.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The attacker controls all hash inputs to the r computation (commitments, cells, proofs, column index) via P2P DataColumnSidecar contents. However, they cannot predict which r value a specific input combination will produce without computing SHA-256 (preimage resistance). The attacker can choose inputs to influence r but cannot reverse-engineer inputs that produce a desired r.
state_anomalies_found: Attacker has full control over r hash inputs via P2P sidecar contents
G1_INFINITY commitments and proofs are accepted by validate_kzg_g1 and would produce a vacuously true pairing check
The all-infinity attack requires a block with all-infinity commitments, blocked by transaction-level validation
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of r. Fresh computation each invocation.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrent state shared in r computation.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: The all-infinity attack scenario is theoretically reachable but blocked by Merkle inclusion proof validation requiring the commitments to match an actual valid block body. No practical exploit path found that bypasses all layers.
attack_scenarios: All-infinity commitments/proofs: passes KZG check vacuously but fails inclusion proof for any real block
SHA-256 preimage search to find inputs producing desired r: 2^128 work, infeasible
Length-extension on hash input: prevented by explicit num_commitments and num_cells length fields

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Attacker controls all variable hash inputs but cannot exploit this control without breaking SHA-256 or KZG. The all-infinity scenario is blocked by upstream checks.
entry_points: P2P DataColumnSidecar with attacker-controlled commitment, cell, proof bytes
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker controls hash inputs but cannot exploit this without breaking SHA-256 preimage resistance.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: r is computationally resistant to attacker influence for the purpose of bypassing the pairing check. SHA-256 preimage resistance prevents targeted r selection. The all-infinity edge case is mitigated by upstream block validation.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: SHA-256 preimage resistance preventing targeted r selection
edge_cases: G1_INFINITY commitments accepted by C library; all-infinity attack needs block-level defense which exists

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: r is computationally resistant to attacker influence. The all-infinity scenario is blocked by upstream validation.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Consider explicitly rejecting G1_INFINITY commitments at the Go layer (VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs) as a defense-in-depth measure.

checklist_item.title: Supporting Check: Can an attacker exploit weak entropy to forge proofs where invalid cells pass batch verification?

audit_items.state_context: Fiat-Shamir transform binds all attacker inputs before r is revealed. Grinding: attacker generates N random triples, computes r for each, checks pairing. For invalid inputs, pairing fails with probability ~1 - 1/p. Need N ~p ~2^254 for one coincidental pass. SHA-256 birthday bound: 2^127. ~9% bias reduces by <0.15 bits.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The ~9% distributional bias in r reduces effective security by less than 0.15 bits (from 2^127 to 2^126.86 for birthday attacks). This is entirely insufficient for a practical attack. All proof forgery paths require either breaking SHA-256 (2^128 work), breaking BLS12-381 DLOG (2^128-2^256 work), or grinding through ~2^127 random inputs.
state_anomalies_found: ~1 bit reduction in effective security from modular bias (negligible)
No other entropy weaknesses found
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching that could reduce effective entropy.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrent state that could reduce effective entropy.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No practical proof forgery path found. Grinding attacks require ~2^127 attempts. Algebraic attacks require breaking BLS12-381 DLOG. Fiat-Shamir attacks require SHA-256 preimage computation. The ~9% bias provides no meaningful advantage to an attacker.
attack_scenarios: Grinding on r: 2^127 attempts needed, infeasible
Birthday attack on r collision: 2^127 sidecars needed, infeasible
Algebraic exploitation of bias: requires BLS DLOG break
Known-answer attack using precomputed r: requires SHA-256 preimage break

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: All forgery paths are computationally infeasible at 127+ bit security levels. The entropy is sufficient.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can influence r through sidecar contents but cannot forge proofs without infeasible computation.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Proof forgery is computationally infeasible. Security level is ~127 bits (limited by SHA-256 birthday bound). The ~9% bias reduces this by negligible <0.15 bits. The protocol is secure under standard cryptographic assumptions.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: SHA-256 (128-bit) + BLS12-381 DLOG (127+ bit) + KZG binding
edge_cases: Quantum attacks reduce BLS security to ~64 bits via Shor's algorithm (protocol-level concern, not code defect)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Entropy is sufficient for proof forgery resistance. No weak entropy vulnerability exists. The ~9% bias is a known, accepted property with negligible security impact.
